nodes.title: Part 1: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 1. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A Linux administrator needs to add a kernel module for a new network card without rebooting the system. The module is called 'e1000e'. Which command accomplishes this?
flashcards.back: modprobe is the correct tool for loading kernel modules because it automatically resolves and loads any module dependencies. insmod can load a module but requires the full path to the .ko file and does not handle dependencies. modinfo only displays information about a module without loading it. lsmod lists currently loaded modules but does not load new ones.

flashcards.front: After a power failure, a server boots into emergency mode with the message 'Failed to mount /data'. The /data partition uses ext4. Which command should the administrator run first to recover the filesystem?
flashcards.back: e2fsck -f forces a filesystem check on an ext4 partition even if it appears clean, which is appropriate after an unclean shutdown. fsck -y would work but -y auto-answers yes to all prompts which can be risky. mount -o remount,rw will fail if the filesystem has errors. xfs_repair is only for XFS filesystems, not ext4.

flashcards.front: A sysadmin wants a new systemd service called 'appd' to start automatically at multi-user.target. Which directive in the [Install] section of the unit file is required?
flashcards.back: WantedBy=multi-user.target in the [Install] section causes systemctl enable to create a symlink in multi-user.target.wants/, making the service start at that target. RequiredBy is not a standard [Install] directive. After= and Requires= belong in [Unit] and control ordering/dependencies but do not enable autostart.

flashcards.front: An administrator needs to create a 10 GB logical volume named 'datalv' in a volume group named 'datavg'. Which command is correct?
flashcards.back: lvcreate -L 10G -n datalv datavg creates a 10 GB logical volume named datalv in the datavg volume group. The -L flag specifies size and -n specifies the name. lvcreate -s creates a snapshot, not a regular LV. vgcreate creates a volume group from physical volumes, not logical volumes. pvcreate initializes a physical volume and does not accept -n or -L in this way.

pairs.option: The -G flag sets the primary group, which was overridden by useradd defaults

nodes.title: Part 2: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 2. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: An administrator wants to prevent a specific kernel module 'pcspkr' from loading at boot. Which method is correct?
flashcards.back: Adding 'blacklist pcspkr' to a file in /etc/modprobe.d/ (such as blacklist.conf) prevents the module from being automatically loaded at boot. This is the persistent, correct method. rmmod removes a currently loaded module but does not prevent future loading. 'install pcspkr /bin/true' is a stronger override (replaces the install command) but is unnecessary for simply blacklisting. /etc/modules is used to load modules at boot, not prevent them.

flashcards.front: A GRUB2 boot entry fails and the system drops to the GRUB rescue prompt. The administrator types 'ls' and sees '(hd0) (hd0,gpt1) (hd0,gpt2)'. Which sequence of commands boots the system?
flashcards.back: From the GRUB rescue prompt, you must set the root device, load the kernel with 'linux', load the initrd, then run 'boot'. The set root command points GRUB to the boot partition. grub-install and update-grub require a running OS. 'insmod normal; normal' is used from the GRUB shell (not rescue) to load the normal module if GRUB modules are available but GRUB's normal mode failed to load. initrd /initrd.img; boot

flashcards.front: A server running RHEL shows the following in 'journalctl -xe': 'kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 3201 (java) score 890'. What is the correct interpretation?
flashcards.back: The OOM (Out of Memory) killer is a kernel mechanism that kills processes when the system has exhausted available memory. The 'score' reflects how aggressively it targets a process (higher = more likely to kill). This is distinct from a Java heap exception (which is a JVM-level error with different log messages), ulimit enforcement (which produces 'Cannot allocate memory' or similar), and cgroup limits (which have different log patterns like 'Memory cgroup limit').

flashcards.front: After rebooting a system, an administrator notices that a custom service file at /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service has been changed on disk but systemd is still using the old version. What must the administrator run?
flashcards.back: systemctl daemon-reload re-reads all unit files from disk without restarting running services, updating systemd's in-memory configuration. Without it, systemd keeps using the cached version of the unit file. After daemon-reload, restarting the service applies the new configuration. systemctl restart without daemon-reload uses the old unit file. systemctl reload sends SIGHUP to reload the service's own configuration (like nginx -s reload), not the unit file. reset-failed clears failed state flags.

pairs.stem: A security audit reveals that /etc/passwd is world-writable. Which command fixes this to the correct permissions (readable by all, writable only by root)?
A server running RHEL shows the following in 'journalctl -xe': 'kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 3201 (java) score 890'. What is the correct interpretation?
pairs.option: A cgroup memory limit was reached and the kernel killed the process to enforce the limit

nodes.title: Part 3: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 3. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: An administrator needs to extract only the third field (colon-delimited) from /etc/passwd to list all usernames. Which command is correct?
flashcards.back: Usernames are in the FIRST field of /etc/passwd. cut -d: -f1 uses colon as delimiter and extracts field 1 (the username). cut -d: -f3 extracts the UID (third field). awk -F: '{print $1}' also extracts the username correctly — but note that option A would be correct for usernames too, while the question asks which of the given commands lists usernames. sed -n '3p' prints the third line of the file, not a field.

flashcards.front: A Bash script must check if a file exists before processing it. Which conditional expression is correct?
flashcards.back: [ -f /etc/config.file ] tests if the path exists AND is a regular file (not a directory or special file). -d tests for a directory, which is wrong for a file. The combination -e (exists) and -x (executable) checks existence and executability, which is not what 'processing a file' generally requires. The test with -r and -w checks read and write permissions, which is more than just 'exists'.

flashcards.front: A script needs to count how many times the word 'ERROR' appears in /var/log/app.log. Which command produces only the count?
flashcards.back: grep -c ERROR /var/log/app.log prints only the count of matching lines directly. grep | wc -l also counts matching lines but requires a pipe. awk counts matching lines too but with more verbosity. While A and B produce the same count for line occurrences, option D is incorrect because awk counts differently if a line has multiple occurrences of ERROR (it counts the line once). grep -c is the most concise single-command solution.

flashcards.front: An administrator needs to replace every occurrence of 'localhost' with '127.0.0.1' in /etc/myapp.conf in place. Which sed command is correct?
flashcards.back: sed -i 's/localhost/127.0.0.1/g' modifies the file in place (-i) and the 'g' flag replaces ALL occurrences on each line. Without -i, sed outputs to stdout and does not modify the file. Without 'g', only the first occurrence per line is replaced. Option D uses incorrect sed syntax (missing 's' substitution command prefix).

nodes.title: Part 4: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 4. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: An administrator uses 'ip route show' and sees 'default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0'. When they try to reach an external server, connections time out. 'ping 192.168.1.1' succeeds. What should the administrator check next?
flashcards.back: The local routing is correct (default gateway is reachable). Since ping to 192.168.1.1 works but external connectivity fails, the problem is upstream from the server: the gateway may lack internet access, or NAT/firewall rules may be blocking outbound traffic. restarting networking won't help since routes are already correct. ip route add 0.0.0.0/0 is redundant since a default route already exists. MTU issues would cause partial connectivity or large packet drops, not complete timeouts from a single hop away.

flashcards.front: A Linux server's /var partition is 100% full, causing application failures. The administrator identifies large rotated logs in /var/log. Which sequence of commands frees space and prevents recurrence?
flashcards.back: Finding and deleting compressed rotated log archives older than 30 days removes old data without risking active log files, then configuring logrotate with size limits prevents recurrence. rm -rf /var/log/* is dangerous as it removes active log files and directory structure. Truncating syslog only frees space from one file without addressing root cause. Bind mounting /tmp to /var/log would hide existing logs and is not a real solution.

flashcards.front: A systemd service 'webapp' keeps failing. Running 'systemctl status webapp' shows 'Active: failed (Result: exit-code)'. Which command shows the detailed failure reason from the service's log output?
flashcards.back: journalctl -u webapp -n 50 shows the last 50 journal entries for the webapp unit, including the process's stdout/stderr output which reveals why it exited with an error. The service may not write to /var/log/webapp.log at all if it's logging to stdout (captured by systemd journal). systemctl show displays unit properties/parameters in machine-readable format, not service output. dmesg shows kernel ring buffer messages, not application logs.

flashcards.front: A user reports they cannot log in with their password. The administrator checks /etc/shadow and sees the account entry as: 'alice:!$6$hash...:19000:0:90:7:::'. What does the '!' prefix on the password hash indicate?
flashcards.back: A '!' (exclamation mark) prepended to the password hash in /etc/shadow locks the account by making the hash invalid. Authentication will fail because no password can produce a hash matching '!hash'. This is what usermod -L does. Two-factor authentication is configured via PAM, not shadow file markers. The hash algorithm is indicated by the $6$ prefix (SHA-512) regardless of the leading !. An unset password would have an empty field or a single '*'.
